title: Training Your Own Late-Interaction Retriever
hook: A domain-specific multi-vector retriever took 14.5 hours on one RTX 3090 and beat every zero-shot model tested — including dense retrievers 33 times its size.
key_points: Sentence Transformers v6.0 adds MultiVectorEncoder plus the training infrastructure to finetune or train ColBERT-style models from scratch.
The author's medical-domain model trained in 14.5 hours on a single RTX 3090 and reached 0.9139 NDCG@10.
It outperformed every zero-shot retriever tested, including dense models 33x larger.
Starting point matters: pre-supervised checkpoints adapt to new domains better than fully finetuned general-purpose models.
Most released multi-vector models truncate documents at 180–512 tokens, so long-document domains lose a lot without custom training.
Index size is manageable — quantization and pooling brought the example index to 1.45GB, smaller than dense alternatives.
content_html: Late-interaction retrieval — one vector per token, scored with MaxSim instead of a single pooled embedding — has been the better-recall option for a while, but training your own has largely been a well-resourced-team activity. Sentence Transformers v6.0 adds a MultiVectorEncoder model type and the training infrastructure around it, and this post walks through actually using it.
extra_html:
The headline experiment

The author finetunes a medical-domain retriever in 14.5 hours on a single RTX 3090, reaching 0.9139 NDCG@10 and beating every zero-shot retriever tested — including dense models 33 times larger. That is the practical argument for domain training in one line: a modest model that has seen your domain beats a big one that has not.

Lessons worth stealing

Which checkpoint you start from matters more than expected. Pre-supervised checkpoints, taken before general-purpose finetuning, adapt to new domains best; putting a fresh projection on a strong backbone ranks second. Watch document length, too — most released multi-vector models truncate at 180 to 512 tokens, so long-document domains lose material silently. And the usual objection, index size, is softer than it looks: quantization and pooling brought the example index to 1.45GB, under the comparable dense setup.

related.title: Multi-Vector Retrieval: One Vector Per Token, Scored Late
related.hook: Squeezing a document into one vector throws away where the match was. Late interaction keeps a vector per token and defers scoring — better recall, 42x the index.

related.title: Why ColBERT-Style Retrieval Fails on Negation — and the Fix
related.hook: Late-interaction retrieval (MaxSim, as in ColBERT) is provably as expressive as vector search for ordinary matches — but provably can't handle negation. Signed MaxSim closes that exact gap.

flashcards.prompt: Why do pre-supervised checkpoints make better starting points for domain finetuning?
flashcards.back_html: They come from before general-purpose finetuning, so they have not yet specialized to a broad retrieval distribution and adapt to a new domain more readily.

flashcards.prompt: What silently hurts multi-vector retrieval on long documents?

choices.text: Most released models truncate documents at 180–512 tokens
MaxSim cannot score documents longer than the query
Token pooling deletes the final tokens of every document
Long documents overflow the index quantizer

flashcards.explanation_html: The truncation limit is a property of the released checkpoints, and everything past it is simply never seen — which is a strong argument for training your own in long-document domains.

flashcards.prompt: Is the index size of a multi-vector retriever prohibitive?
flashcards.back_html: Not necessarily. Raw indexes look large, but quantization and pooling brought the post's example down to 1.45GB — smaller than the comparable dense setup.
